title: What is a hangover, really?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore what causes a hangover and what actually helps. They open with a warning about drinking under twenty-one and personal hangover anecdotes, then cover the medical term "veisalgia" and a Bible verse (Isaiah 5:11). Causes covered: vasopressin suppression and the diuretic effect, dehydration and brain shrinkage, loss of electrolytes, glycogen depletion, glutamine overproduction and poor sleep, congeners and darker liquors, and acetaldehyde toxicity with glutathione and cysteine, which women have less of. They discuss why beer before liquor advice is questionable, age-related hangover severity, and vomiting as the body's response. Remedies discussed include hair of the dog (debunked), coffee, fatty food, bananas, eggs, fruit juice, water with salt and sugar, aspirin and ibuprofen, over-the-counter hangover pills, and pacing drinks with water. The episode ends with a listener mail from Mark, a former 2000 Census enumerator, plus Kiva and sign-off notes.

segments.title: Opening banter and hangover anecdotes
segments.summary: Hosts open with an under-21 drinking warning and trade personal stories about drinking and hangovers.

segments.title: Veisalgia and a Bible verse on hangovers
segments.summary: The medical term for hangover, veisalgia, is explained as Norwegian and Greek roots, and Isaiah 5:11 is quoted about rising early to follow strong drink.

segments.title: Vasopressin, diuresis, and dehydration
segments.summary: Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, so the kidneys send water to the bladder and the body loses far more fluid than it takes in, causing dehydration and a headache. The hosts also describe brain shrinkage pulling on the meninges.

segments.title: Electrolytes, glycogen, and glutamine
segments.summary: Hangovers deplete electrolytes such as salt, potassium and magnesium and glycogen, causing weakness and fatigue. Alcohol also blocks glutamine production, and the body overproduces it after drinking, disrupting sleep.

segments.title: Congeners, darker liquors, and acetaldehyde
segments.summary: Darker liquors contain more impurities and tend to cause heavier hangovers, with a study comparing bourbon and vodka. Acetaldehyde, a liver byproduct more toxic than alcohol, is neutralized by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase and glutathione with cysteine, which women have less of.

segments.title: Beer before liquor and age effects
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the rhyme about beer before liquor, carbonation speeding alcohol absorption, and the hosts' observation that hangovers worsen around age twenty-four.

segments.title: Vomiting as a response to alcohol
segments.summary: Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, which secretes hydrochloric acid and triggers vomiting through hormonal signals to the brain. The hosts note that self-induced vomiting can be dangerous and signal a drinking problem.

segments.title: Hangover cures overview and hair of the dog
segments.summary: The hosts say some cures are real because they replace what was lost. Hair of the dog is debunked, since a drink the next morning only adds toxins.

segments.title: Food, coffee, fruit juice, and aspirin remedies
segments.summary: Coffee eases headaches but dehydrates. Fatty food may coat the stomach, bananas supply potassium, eggs supply cysteine, and water with sugar and salt helps. Fruit juice is suggested as a sugar source. Aspirin, taken before bed and on waking, is suggested, with a warning about stomach upset. Ethanol-type remedies and Kiva-style caveats are noted.

segments.title: Hosts' personal cures and over-the-counter hangover pills
segments.summary: Hosts share personal cures: sleeping in after aspirin and ibuprofen plus water, and Coca-Cola. They describe over-the-counter hangover pills as mainly vitamins and water, and advise drinking water between drinks and moderation.

segments.title: Gin, tequila, and red wine behavior
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how different liquors affect behavior, including gin, tequila and red wine, and an anecdote about Alexander the Great's death after a wine-drinking contest.

segments.title: HowStuffWorks article and Kiva promotion
segments.summary: Hosts recommend the How Hangovers Work article and promote Kiva microloans.

segments.title: Listener mail from former census enumerator
segments.summary: Mark, a former 2000 Census enumerator from Fishkill, New York, describes door-to-door visits, hostile residents, and friendly grandmothers. He also notes he was unaware enumerators had been killed.
